messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard deviation (i.e., the standard error) of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis is  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.221.
\]
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? Usually we compute the standard error: sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That would be sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). Let's compute: sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So standard error ~0.221.

But they might want to calculate the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic under null is sqrt((n-1)/(n-3))? Actually the t distribution has variance n-1/(n-3) for n>3. But maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null: that's the standard error. So answer: 0.221.

But the user specifically says "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They might want to compute the standard deviation of the test statistic? But they didn't ask for p-value or t-statistic. They just want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. That is ambiguous. But likely they want the standard error of the mean under null: sqrt((sample_std_dev^2)/sample_size). So 1.4^2 = 1.96. Divided by 40 = 0.049. sqrt(0.049) = 0.221. So answer: 0.221.

We can also mention that the standard error is 0.221. So the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null is 0.221. So answer: 0.221.

Thus we respond with the standard error.
